title: The Bike Lane Budget
subtitle: Rates, Percents and a Planning Decision
summary: The fictional city of Harlow can fund one protected bike lane. Listen to a planning meeting, read a memo, a cost table and a chart, compare the streets with percents and rates, then explain and write a recommendation.

briefing.scene: The city of Harlow has $400,000 to build one protected bike lane. Three streets are on the list, and each one costs more than half of the budget. As the Junior Planner, you must compare the numbers before Friday's meeting.
briefing.goal: Use percents, ratios and rates to compare the three streets, then explain your method and recommend one street in writing.

turns.speaker: Ms. Mbeki
turns.text: Thank you for coming. We have a budget of $400,000 for one protected bike lane this year. Each street costs more than half of the budget, so we can build only one. Mr. Okoye, please share the counts.

turns.speaker: Mr. Okoye
turns.text: Yes. Park Avenue has the most riders today, 410 trips on a weekday. Mill Street has 240, and Cedar Road has 120. Our surveys suggest trips would grow by 30 percent on Park Avenue, 50 percent on Mill Street, and 100 percent on Cedar Road. Cedar Road is the longest lane at three miles, and it costs the least per mile, at $100,000.

turns.speaker: Ms. Hoffman
turns.text: Thank you. My school is on Mill Street, and about one in four of our 480 students cross it to get to class. Last year there were 6 crashes involving bicycles on Mill Street and 2 on Park Avenue. Rider counts alone do not show where people face the most danger.

turns.speaker: Ms. Mbeki
turns.text: Thank you both. Before Friday, please compare the cost per added trip and the safety record, and bring me a recommendation.

memo.title: Planning Department Memo: Comparing Bike Lane Projects
text: When two projects have different lengths and costs, total cost alone does not show which one gives more value. Planners therefore compare rates.

A cost per mile compares price to length. A cost per added trip divides the total cost by the number of new weekday trips the lane is expected to create. A percent increase is applied to today's trips: for example, a 50 percent increase on 240 trips adds 120 trips.

A lower cost per added trip means each dollar is expected to bring more riders. However, rates do not measure safety. Planners also review crash records and the number of students who cross each street.

phases.title: Planning Meeting: One Lane, Three Streets
phases.instructions: Listen to part of the planning meeting. Three people speak. Listen for the budget, the counts and the safety concern.

tasks.q: Why can the city build only one bike lane this year?

options.text: All three streets together cost less than the budget.
Cedar Road is the longest street at three miles.
The city council allows only one construction project a year.
Each street costs more than half of the $400,000 budget.

tasks.explain: Ms. Mbeki says the budget is $400,000 and 'each street costs more than half of the budget, so we can build only one.' Cedar Road's length is a true detail but not the reason.

tasks.q: Why does Ms. Hoffman say rider counts alone are not enough?

options.text: Her school has 480 students on Mill Street.
Rider counts are never useful for any kind of planning.
Counts do not show where the most danger is.
Mill Street had 6 crashes involving bicycles last year.

tasks.explain: Ms. Hoffman ends with 'Rider counts alone do not show where people face the most danger.' The crash count is part of her evidence, but it is not her reason. She says 'alone,' not 'never useful.'

tasks.q: Choose the statements that support the claim: 'Mill Street has a safety concern.'

pool.text: about one in four of our 480 students cross it to get to class
Last year there were 6 crashes involving bicycles on Mill Street and 2 on Park Avenue.
Rider counts alone do not show where people face the most danger.
Park Avenue has the most riders today, 410 trips on a weekday.
Cedar Road is the longest lane at three miles
We have a budget of $400,000 for one protected bike lane this year.

phases.title: Compare the Projects with Rates
phases.instructions: Read the planning memo, the cost table and the growth chart. Use the numbers to compare the three streets.

tasks.q: According to the memo, what does 'cost per added trip' tell planners?

options.text: Dollars spent for each new weekday trip.
How many miles of bike lane each dollar buys.
Which street is the safest for students to cross.
How much money the city earns from each new rider.

tasks.explain: The memo says a cost per added trip 'divides the total cost by the number of new weekday trips.' Miles per dollar would be the opposite of cost per mile. The memo also says rates do not measure safety.

tasks.q: After the lane opens, how many weekday bike trips are expected on Park Avenue?

options.text: 123 trips
440 trips
533 trips

tasks.explain: The chart shows a 30 percent increase. 30 percent of 410 is 123 added trips, and 410 + 123 = 533. The 123 is only the increase; 440 adds 30 trips instead of 30 percent.

tasks.q: Which statement about Mill Street and Cedar Road is supported by the table and chart?

options.text: Mill Street is expected to add more trips than Cedar Road.
A bigger percent increase always means more new trips.
Both are expected to add the same number of trips: 120.
Cedar Road costs the least per mile of the three streets.

tasks.explain: 50 percent of Mill Street's 240 trips is 120, and 100 percent of Cedar Road's 120 trips is 120. A larger percent applied to a smaller number can give the same result. Cedar Road's low cost per mile is true but does not answer the question.

tasks.q: Which street has the lowest cost per added trip?

options.text: Park Avenue, because it has the most riders today.
Mill Street, at $3,000 per added trip.
All three are the same, because each adds about 120 trips.
Cedar Road, at $2,500 per added trip.

tasks.explain: Mill Street: $360,000 / 120 = $3,000. Park Avenue: $336,000 / 123 is about $2,732. Cedar Road: $300,000 / 120 = $2,500. The added trips are about equal, but the total costs are different.

tasks.q: Engineers revise Park Avenue's expected growth from 30 percent to 40 percent. How many weekday trips would the lane add?

options.text: 164 trips
574 trips
450 trips
123 trips

tasks.explain: 40 percent of 410 is 0.40 x 410 = 164 added trips. 574 is the new total (410 + 164), not the added trips. 450 adds 40 trips instead of 40 percent. 123 was the answer for 30 percent.

tasks.q: Mr. Okoye might recommend Cedar Road for its low cost per added trip. Which statement gives the best reason to weigh something besides cost?

options.text: Cedar Road has had more crashes than the other two streets.
Park Avenue is expected to have the most weekday trips afterward.
Cost per added trip ignores safety, and Mill Street had 6 crashes.
The memo says cost per added trip should be ignored completely.

tasks.explain: The memo says rates 'do not measure safety,' and Ms. Hoffman reports 6 crashes on Mill Street. No crash data is given for Cedar Road. The memo does not say to ignore rates; it says to review safety as well.

phases.title: Choose the Next Analysis
phases.instructions: You can request one more piece of analysis before Friday's meeting. Choose one. Either choice leads to a complete mission.

decision.q: Which analysis do you request first?

options.text: Ask Ms. Hoffman for the school's crossing counts
options.consequence: The counts show that far more students cross Mill Street than the other two streets. A safety argument for Mill Street gets stronger, even though its cost per added trip is the highest.

board.label: Crossing counts
board.text: 120 students cross Mill Street each weekday, compared with 45 on Park Avenue and 15 on Cedar Road.

board.label: Crossing counts
board.text: Mill Street has the most students crossing and the most recorded crashes (6).

options.text: Ask Mr. Okoye for the expected trips after each lane opens
options.consequence: The totals show that Park Avenue would carry far more trips than the others. A ridership argument for Park Avenue gets stronger, even though Cedar Road is cheaper per added trip.

board.label: Expected trips
board.text: After the lanes open: Park Avenue 533 trips, Mill Street 360, Cedar Road 240.

board.label: Expected trips
board.text: Park Avenue would have more than twice as many trips as Cedar Road (533 compared with 240).

phases.title: Open House: Explain Your Method
phases.instructions: Explain your comparison to a resident. Use the table and the numbers on your board.

task.title: Explain the Comparison
task.scenario: A resident at the planning open house asks, 'How do you decide which street is the better deal?' You have one minute to explain your method.
task.prompt: Explain how to compare two bike lanes using cost per added trip. Show the steps for one street with its numbers, then say which of the two streets costs less for each added trip.

planner.label: Step 1: added trips
planner.hint: Find the percent of today's trips.

planner.label: Step 2: divide
planner.hint: Divide the total cost by the added trips.

planner.label: Step 3: compare
planner.hint: Say which street costs less per added trip.

planner.label: My caution
planner.hint: Name one thing the rate does not tell us.

frames: First, I find the added trips by ___.
That gives about ___ per added trip.
___ costs less for each added trip, but the rate does not show ___.
guided.model: First, I find the added trips. For Cedar Road, 100 percent of 120 trips is 120 added trips. Then I divide the total cost, $300,000, by 120. That gives $2,500 per added trip. For Park Avenue, 30 percent of 410 is 123 added trips, and $336,000 divided by 123 is about $2,732. Cedar Road costs less for each added trip, but the rate does not show safety.

successCriteria: I show the steps in order with words such as 'first' and 'then'.
I say each number with its unit (dollars, trips, percent).
I compare two streets with 'costs less' or 'costs more'.
I name one thing the rate does not show.

listenFor: Percent of today's trips correctly used to find added trips
Division of total cost by added trips
A comparison sentence, not only two separate answers
teacher.followUp: Why do we divide the cost by the added trips and not by today's trips?

plannerHint.s4: Use the expected trips: the rate does not show which street carries the most riders.

task.scenario: Director Mbeki has asked for your recommendation before Friday. She will share your email with the planning team, so it must be clear about the numbers.
task.prompt: Write an email that recommends which street should get the bike lane. Compare at least two streets using a rate, and explain one thing the rate cannot tell the team.

frames: Dear Director Mbeki, I recommend ___ because ___.
Compared with ___, ___ costs ___ per added trip.
However, the rate does not show ___.
For that reason, I suggest that the team ___.
guided.model:
Dear Director Mbeki, I recommend Cedar Road because it gives the most added trips for each dollar. Compared with Mill Street, which costs $3,000 per added trip, Cedar Road costs $2,500 per added trip.

However, the rate does not show safety. Ms. Hoffman reported 6 crashes on Mill Street last year, so the team should review crash records before it votes. For that reason, I suggest that we ask for the crash data for Cedar Road as well.

revisionPrompts.prompt: Does every number have a unit (dollars, trips, crashes)? Add the unit where it is missing.
Replace 'cheap' or 'good' with a rate and the numbers behind it.
Add 'However' or 'For that reason' to connect the rate to your caution.

successCriteria: I name one street in my first sentence.
I compare two streets with a rate and write each number with its unit.
I explain one thing the rate cannot show.

lookFor: A recommendation that names a street
A limitation of the rate (such as safety)
commonIssues: Using total cost instead of cost per added trip
Treating the lowest rate as the only factor

teacherQuestions: How did you find the number of added trips from a percent increase? Show one example.
Why can two streets add the same number of trips even when their percent increases are different?
What did the extra analysis you requested (crossing counts or expected trips) change about your recommendation?
debrief.connections: Connect to ratios and rates: unit rate, percent of a quantity, and comparing quantities with different sizes. Ask students when a rate is useful and when a rate hides important information such as safety or fairness.
